newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU wrestling with legal base for EMU.
newsitem.headline: EU wrestling with legal base for EMU.

text.p: European Union monetary officials are struggling to reach a compromise on how to establish a legal base for a single currency well in advance of its expected launch in 1999.

While the European Commission, the EU's executive, has won praise from financial institutions on its draft legal framework, putting it into effect quickly so that any doubts over future financial obligations are put to rest, is proving difficult.
"I think this is an issue that the Commission's lawyers will have to solve," said one EU official.

The root of the problem, one that left the EU's monetary committee groping for answers earlier this week, is which part of the Maastricht Treaty would be best suited for implementing the legal base -- Article 109L4 or Article 235.

Article 109L4 addresses questions of legality and the conversion of national currencies into the new currency, the euro. The problem is that it stipulates such decisions can only become EU law at the start of European monetary and economic union (EMU) in 1999.

For many, a delay in establishing the legal certainty for the continuity of financial contracts, for example, could undermine private sector confidence in EMU and slow the necessary and costly changeover process for many companies.
"With many of these things the financial markets have a strong interest in getting them settled now," says Graham Bishop, an economist at Salomon Brothers in London.

The alternative to Article 109L4 is to use Article 235, which in the case of EMU essentially says that any decision falling outside the Maastricht framework for monetary union would require the unanimous backing of all 15 member states.
It is an option many countries would prefer to sidestep.
"There are a number of states which have a general objection to use Article 235," said one official.
Others say the urgency expressed by some critics is overblown and unwarranted, particularly since a decision on which countries join EMU will not be known until early 1998.
Some legal experts argue that a legal base for EMU, while important, should not be viewed as an absolute necessity in order to protect investors.

There are significant differences between the way English law and Roman law practised in Continental Europe operate. Even if Britain was to stick to its right to opt out of EMU, legal jurisdiction could remain an issue as a high proportion of financial trading is carried out in London.
But both English and international law already have adequate provisions to deal with the legal uncertainties that may arise under the changeover to a single currency.

A recent study by Norton Rose, a London law firm, said EMU cannot result in the frustration or termination of a financial contract merely on the ground that it is expressed in a national currency which participates in the changeover to a single currency.
Monetary officials say it is unlikely that the matter will be resolved when EU finance ministers and central bank governors meet informally in Dublin on September 20 and 21.
